What the official sources say

  • Petitions to the county property value appeals board are filed with the board clerk after tax statements are mailed and by December 31. (ORS 309.100(2); source)
  • The board hears petitions to reduce real market value, assessed value, or maximum assessed value as of January 1. (ORS 309.026(2); source)
  • If a taxpayer may appeal to the property value appeals board, no Tax Court appeal is allowed until the board order issues; Tax Court appeal is from the board order. (ORS 305.275(3); source)
  • Real and personal property is valued at 100 percent of real market value; assessed value is generally the lesser of maximum assessed value or real market value. (ORS 308.232; 308.146; source)
  • Maximum assessed value equals 103 percent of prior-year assessed value or 100 percent of prior-year maximum assessed value, whichever is greater. (ORS 308.146(1); source)
  • A person aggrieved by an omitted-property assessment may appeal to the Tax Court within 90 days after the roll correction. (ORS 311.223(4); source)
  • Real property is subject to tax foreclosure when three years have elapsed from the earliest delinquency. (ORS 312.010(1); source)
  • The county holds foreclosed property for two years from the judgment date unless redeemed. (ORS 312.120(1); source)

How is an Oregon property tax bill built?

Oregon bills each home on an assessed value that usually sits below its market value. The system comes from two ballot measures. Measure 5 (1990) keeps operating taxes at or below $15 per $1,000 of real market value, and voter-approved bonds fall outside that limit.

Measure 50 passed in May 1997 and changed how value is counted. According to Clatsop County's explanation, first-year assessed value was set at the 1995 value minus 10 percent, and after that it can grow no more than 3 percent a year. Each taxing district also received a permanent rate that limits its operating tax authority.

Assessed value rises faster than 3 percent only in a short list of cases:

  • New improvements
  • Subdivisions and rezoning
  • Disqualification from a special assessment or exemption
  • Omitted property

Minor construction and ordinary maintenance are not added to assessed value. The tax year runs July 1 to June 30, and the assessment date is January 1.

Who sets and collects property tax in Oregon?

The county assessor. The Department of Revenue's property page states that property taxes are set by and paid to the county assessor, and that the department itself does not hold most residential and commercial property records.

The state agency handles centrally assessed companies and state-appraised industrial property. It also runs programs that matter to homeowners: the deferral program for disabled and senior homeowners, the forestland program, and the Property Value Appeals Board contacts. For questions about one house, the department sends owners back to the county. Its phone line is 503-378-4988, or 800-356-4222.

Oregon has 36 counties, so there are 36 assessor offices, each with its own website, payment options and forms. Multnomah, Washington and Clackamas lead the population list, while Wheeler, Gilliam and Sherman are the smallest.

When are Oregon property taxes due, and what do late payments cost?

The first installment is due November 15. The collector must mail or deliver statements by October 25 (ORS 311.250), and the schedule itself is in ORS 311.505.

ItemRule
Pay everything by Nov. 153 percent discount
Pay two-thirds by Nov. 152 percent discount on that portion, final third due May 15
Pay one-third by Nov. 15No discount, then Feb. 15 and May 15
Late interest1 1/3 percent per month or part of a month, starting Dec. 15, Feb. 15 or May 15 for the matching installment
Bills under $40No installments, pay in full
Lien date for real propertyJuly 1 of the levy year, until paid (ORS 311.405)

Multnomah County's payment FAQ adds details: if the 15th lands on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day; payments are credited to the earliest tax year still owed; and a returned check carries a $25 fee and can cost the discount. Other counties may differ on those points.

What happens to the property tax bill when a house is sold?

The tax follows the property, so any unpaid amount has to be settled at or before closing. Because the lien attaches on July 1 of the levy year, a sale in the middle of the fiscal year involves both taxes already billed and taxes that have not yet come due.

Multnomah County explains that a yellow tax bill means a mortgage company or a deferral program requested the information and may pay it. An owner who paid off a loan, changed lenders or cancelled a tax reserve should use that bill to pay directly. The same page says it does not cover how escrow handles payoff at closing, and sends owners to the county assessment office or the mortgage company.

Missed installments carry the monthly interest shown above, so confirming the balance with the county before listing avoids surprises at closing.

Does Oregon's senior and disability tax deferral affect a sale?

Yes. The state holds a lien for the deferred taxes plus interest, and a sale makes the balance due. The Oregon statutes in ORS chapter 311 set the rules for the homestead deferral.

  • Applicants must be 62 or older by April 15 of the claim year, or have a disability, which means receiving or being eligible for federal Social Security disability or blindness benefits.
  • Combined household income for the prior year must be under $70,000, and net worth under $500,000, not counting the home.
  • The home must have been the claimant's homestead for at least five years, with exceptions.
  • Claims are filed between January 1 and April 15 before the tax year. Late claims run through December 1 with a fee.
  • Interest is 6 percent a year on taxes the state advanced.

Repayment comes due on the claimant's death, a sale or transfer of the property, loss of homestead status, or removal of a manufactured or floating home from Oregon. Payment is generally due by August 15 of the year after the event. Anyone who inherits the house may be jointly liable up to the property's equity, and the lien can be foreclosed like a purchase money mortgage.

A reverse mortgage generally blocks the program. Mortgage clauses that bar a homeowner from applying for deferral are void.

What happens if Oregon property taxes go unpaid for years?

After three years, the county can foreclose. ORS 312.010 says real property is subject to foreclosure three years after the earliest delinquency date of the taxes levied.

The process gives the owner several chances to step in:

  • Notice goes by one newspaper publication and by delivery to owners of record, and the county must try to locate them.
  • The notice states the exact amount owed and describes the deferral programs.
  • The county holds the property two years from judgment. Eligible redeemers include prior owners, heirs, lienholders of record and municipalities.
  • Redeeming costs the full judgment amount, interest, a 5 percent penalty and a fee of $50, or the greater of $50 and the title search cost once the one-year notice has gone out.
  • At least a year before redemption ends, the tax collector must send certified and first-class mail with the amount owed, the end date, surplus rights and relief programs.

The former owner keeps possession during redemption, but waste on the property forfeits that right.

Who gets the money if the county sells a foreclosed Oregon home?

The former owner, or the owner's estate and heirs, if anything is left after the county's costs. ORS 312.520 to 312.560 lay out the steps.

If the house was the former owner's primary residence in a residential zone, the county must list it with a licensed agent, and it needs an appraisal when its real market value is above $250,000. An auction follows if the property does not sell after three broker attempts or within 12 months. Auction rules include advertising for at least 30 days and a minimum bid of two-thirds of fair market value.

The surplus equals the property's value less allowable county costs, and the county must determine it within 60 days of the proceeds being deposited. Claims run through the State Treasurer, and heirs can claim without probate under listed conditions. Claimants have no interest in the surplus during the redemption period, and foreclosure does not erase the owner's other debts.

That makes timing important. Redeeming before the period ends keeps the house out of a county sale, and the owner keeps whatever equity remains.

More questions about Oregon Property Tax Guide

When are Oregon property taxes due?

November 15, February 15 and May 15, in three installments. Paying all of it by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount, and paying two-thirds earns 2 percent on that part. Interest on late amounts is 1 1/3 percent per month.

Who do I call about my Oregon property tax bill?

Your county assessor. The state Department of Revenue says property taxes are set by and paid to the county assessor, and it does not keep most home records. The department can be reached at 503-378-4988 for state-level programs.

Can I defer my Oregon property taxes if I am retired?

Possibly. You must be 62 or older, or have a qualifying disability, and your household income must be under $70,000 with net worth under $500,000, among other tests. The state files a lien and charges 6 percent interest, and the balance comes due when you sell.

How long before Oregon can foreclose on unpaid property taxes?

Three years after the earliest delinquency date. After judgment, the county holds the property for two years, during which the owner or heirs can redeem it.

Does Oregon tax assessed value or market value?

Both appear in the system. Operating taxes are capped at $15 per $1,000 of real market value, and assessed value can grow only 3 percent a year in most cases.

What the official sources say

  • For child support, spousal support or restitution judgments the homestead exemption is $40,000 ($50,000 combined). (ORS 18.395(1)(b); source)
  • The homestead must be the actual abode of and occupied by the owner or the owner's spouse, parent or child. (ORS 18.395(1)(c); source)
  • The exemption is effective without a claim by the judgment debtor and extends to sale proceeds held up to one year with intent to buy another homestead. (ORS 18.395(1)(a),(2); source)
  • The exemption applies to a manufactured dwelling, floating home, and a purchaser's interest under a land sale contract. (ORS 18.395(9),(10); source)
  • Separate from the creditor exemption, Oregon offers property tax deferral on an owner-occupied homestead for qualifying seniors/persons with a disability (ORS 311.666 to 311.701). (ORS 311.666; source)

What does the Oregon homestead exemption actually protect?

Oregon's homestead exemption shields part of the value of the home you live in from a creditor who holds a court judgment. It is a debt-collection rule found in ORS 18.395, and it is separate from any property tax break. Oregon does not make you file anything to get it, because it applies by operation of law.

Two things matter to a seller. The exemption covers only a dollar slice of the equity, so a house worth far more than the slice can still be reached by a judgment creditor. And it follows the home through a sale only if the money is handled the right way afterward.

How much is the Oregon homestead exemption now?

For a single judgment debtor the exemption is $158,300 from July 1, 2026 until July 1, 2027, and $316,700 for two or more judgment debtors in the same household. The Oregon Judicial Department publishes a table of the amounts, which now adjust each July 1.

Effective dateOne judgment debtorTwo or more in a household
Before January 1, 2025$40,000$50,000
January 1, 2025 to June 30, 2025$150,000$300,000
July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026$154,200$308,400
July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027$158,300$316,700
July 1, 2027 onwardSet by the State Court AdministratorSet by the State Court Administrator

Older printed copies of the statute and many websites still show $40,000 and $50,000. Those figures applied only before 2025, so check the court's adjustment table before you rely on a number.

Who qualifies and what property counts?

The home must be the actual residence of the owner, or of the owner's spouse, parent or child, and it must be occupied by that person. A temporary absence with the intent to return does not cost you the exemption.

  • The exemption reaches a purchaser's interest under a land sale contract.
  • It applies to manufactured dwellings and floating homes as defined in Oregon law.
  • ORS 18.402 limits the size of the homestead to 160 acres outside a platted town or city, or one block inside one.
  • The exemption can apply to property located outside Oregon, according to an annotation citing a federal bankruptcy decision.

The full text of ORS 18.395 also covers what happens when the owner moves or sells. In that case the exemption continues for one year from the earliest of those events, which gives a household time to buy a replacement.

Which debts can still reach an Oregon homestead?

The exemption does not stop four kinds of claims: construction liens, purchase money liens, lawfully executed mortgages, and a seller's enforcement of rights under a land sale contract. Those are listed in ORS 18.406.

The statute annotations add that a lien from a property division judgment in a divorce under ORS 107.105 is an exception to the exemption as well. A mortgage lender, a contractor who improved the property and a spouse with a property division lien are therefore not held back by it.

Property tax is a different matter. A county can foreclose for delinquent taxes after three years from the earliest date of delinquency, according to ORS 312.010. A homeowner who is behind on taxes and also facing a judgment has two separate clocks running.

How does the exemption work when a house with a judgment lien is sold?

A judgment against an owner can become a lien on real property in the county where the judgment is entered, but only if the court administrator notes in the register that it creates one. The lien reaches property the debtor owns when the judgment is entered and property acquired later, until the lien expires.

A seller who wants a clean closing can use the process in ORS 18.412. After signing an agreement to transfer a homestead, the owner or the buyer can send the judgment creditor a notice of intent to discharge the lien.

  • The notice goes by certified mail to the creditor.
  • It must describe the property and the judgment, state the fair market value and list each encumbrance.
  • It sets an objection date no earlier than 14 days after mailing.
  • If the property is worth more than senior liens plus the exemption, the excess, or the judgment amount if smaller, must be deposited with the court.
  • If the creditor does not object by the date, the property may be discharged from the lien without further notice.

If the creditor objects, the court decides the value or the other issues under ORS 18.415. The notice has to state the value and every encumbrance, so consider having an attorney prepare it.

What happens to sale proceeds under the homestead rule?

The exemption can carry over to the money from a sale, but only if the proceeds are held for no more than one year and held with the intent to buy another homestead. That one-year window is in ORS 18.395.

For someone selling a house to settle debts, the practical lesson is to keep the sale proceeds separate and documented. Keeping a clear record is the easiest way to show the money was set aside for a new home. A bankruptcy attorney can explain how a case changes the picture, and the statute also fixes the home's value for these purposes at the earlier of the bankruptcy petition date or the transfer date.

Is there a separate property tax deferral in Oregon?

Yes. The state runs a property tax deferral for disabled and senior homeowners in which the State of Oregon pays the county property taxes each November 15 and places a lien on the home. It has nothing to do with creditor protection, and it has to be repaid when the home is sold.

Item2026 detail
Household income limit$70,000 for 2025 income
Home value limitReal market value must fall within the county and years-of-residence limits, or under the $301,000 minimum cap
Interest on deferred taxes6 percent simple interest per year
Application deadlineApril 15 with the county assessor
Late applicationApril 16 to December 1, with a fee of 10 percent of taxes, between $20 and $180
RecertificationEvery two years

The Department of Revenue says the lien is released about eight weeks after a payoff posts, and that a payoff received by October 30 can stop the state from paying that November's taxes if ownership changes after September 1. Details are on the Department of Revenue deferral page.

Do disabled veterans get a homestead property tax exemption?

Oregon offers a veteran's property tax exemption for an honorably discharged veteran with a 40 percent disability and for the unmarried surviving spouse of a veteran. The applicant or spouse must own the home and the applicant must live there.

Deschutes County tells applicants to file with the assessor between January 1 and April 1 for the following tax year. An income limit applies only when the disability is documented by a private physician instead of the VA. The county page does not give a dollar amount, so confirm the current exemption with your own county assessor.

More questions about Oregon Homestead Exemption

How much is the Oregon homestead exemption in 2026?

$158,300 for one judgment debtor and $316,700 for two or more in the same household, for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. The Oregon Judicial Department lists the exact figures and the date each took effect.

Do I have to file a claim to get the Oregon homestead exemption?

No. The exemption is effective without a claim by the judgment debtor, so it applies automatically. Anyone facing a judgment sale or a lien discharge should ask an attorney how to raise it in that proceeding.

Does the homestead exemption protect my house from my mortgage lender?

No. ORS 18.406 says the exemption does not apply to lawfully executed mortgages, purchase money liens, construction liens or a seller's rights under a land sale contract.

How long can I hold the sale proceeds of my home and keep the exemption?

Up to one year, and only if you hold the money with the intent to buy another homestead. The year runs from the earliest of the move, absence or sale.

What is the Oregon property tax deferral income limit?

For 2026 the household income limit is $70,000, counting taxable and non-taxable income of the applicant and a spouse living in the home for calendar year 2025. The state charges 6 percent simple interest on the taxes it pays for you.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Oregon imposes an estate tax on transfers by resident decedents and on nonresidents owning Oregon real or tangible personal property. (ORS 118.010(2); source)
  • Oregon's rate table begins at a taxable estate of $1,000,000 at 10.0 percent and rises to 16.0 percent above $9,500,000. (ORS 118.010(4); source)
  • The Oregon taxable estate starts from the federal taxable estate, adjusted by statute. (ORS 118.010(3); source)
  • An Oregon special marital property election is made by the executor on the estate tax return. (ORS 118.016(1); source)
Selling in Oregon?

Does Oregon have an estate tax, and when does an estate owe it?

Yes. Oregon charges an estate transfer tax when the gross estate at death is $1 million or more and includes property Oregon can tax. The Department of Revenue says a return is required at that level, and the tax is imposed on every resident decedent and on nonresidents who own Oregon real or tangible personal property (ORS 118.010).

The executor files, not the heirs. For a probated estate that is the court-appointed personal representative, and for a non-probate estate it is anyone holding the property. The return for deaths on or after January 1, 2012 is Form OR-706, and the older Form IT-1 was used for earlier deaths.

The $1 million line is not indexed for inflation. Real estate and retirement accounts both count toward it, which can surprise families who assume only large estates are covered.

What are the Oregon estate tax rates?

Oregon uses graduated rates that start at 10 percent on the part of the taxable estate over $1 million and rise to 16 percent above $9.5 million. The tax is the base amount for the bracket plus the rate on the excess over its lower limit.

Taxable estate overBase taxRate on excess

$1,500,000$50,00010.25%
$2,500,000$152,50010.5%
$3,500,000$257,50011.0%
$4,500,000$367,50011.5%
$5,500,000$482,50012.0%
$6,500,000$602,50013.0%
$7,500,000$732,50014.0%
$8,500,000$872,50015.0%
$9,500,000$1,022,50016.0%

The department's instructions give an example: a $1,450,000 gross estate with $20,000 of deductions has a $1,430,000 taxable estate. On the table above, the tax on that figure is $43,000, which is 10 percent of the $430,000 over the first million.

How is the Oregon taxable estate calculated?

It starts with the federal taxable estate and is then adjusted by statute. The statute adds back state death taxes deductible under federal law, and subtracts the value of Oregon special marital property and qualifying natural resource property, among other items.

  • Bequests to a surviving spouse can be deducted, and a marital or QTIP claim needs an Oregon-only Schedule M.
  • An executor may make an Oregon special marital property election on the return, and elections made for state purposes are irrevocable.
  • The second spouse's estate must include property previously claimed for a QTIP or special marital deduction.

For a resident with property in other states, the table amount is multiplied by a ratio. The numerator is Oregon real and tangible property plus intangibles, and the denominator is the gross estate. For a nonresident, only Oregon real and tangible property goes in the numerator, which is why an out-of-state owner of an Oregon rental or cabin can face an Oregon filing.

When is the Oregon estate tax return due?

For deaths on or after January 1, 2022, the return and payment are due 12 months after the date of death. For earlier deaths the deadline was nine months, and the department's instructions from that period still use that figure in the body of the text.

ItemWhat the department says
Return requiredGross estate of $1 million or more
Due date, death on or after 1/1/202212 months after death
Extension to fileSix months, using Form OR-706 EXT
Extension to payOnly in special circumstances, under OAR 150-118-0150
Fiduciary income returnForm OR-41 if a probated estate had any gross income

An extension to file does not extend the time to pay, and interest runs on unpaid tax. The department's 2021 instructions describe a 5 percent penalty for late filing or payment, rising to 25 percent in total when the return is more than three months late. Payment is made to the Department of Revenue, which gives a receipt to whoever pays (ORS 118.250).

If you are late on a return or unsure about a date of death, call the Estate/Fiduciary Tax Unit at 503-378-4988 before the deadline passes.

How does an Oregon estate tax affect selling the inherited house?

The house is part of the gross estate at its date-of-death value, and that same value generally becomes the heir's basis. IRS Publication 551 says inherited property basis is generally fair market value at the date of death, or the alternate valuation date if the personal representative elected it.

That has a direct benefit for sellers. If the home is sold soon after the death at about the appraised value, there is often little or no income gain to report, even if the owner bought it decades ago.

The estate may still have a cash problem. A house can be the largest asset in a taxable estate while the tax is due in cash, and the department's instructions describe installment payment of the tax with a first mortgage on Oregon real property as possible collateral. If the extension to pay runs more than 12 months, the estate must provide collateral equal to twice the unpaid tax.

We could not confirm from the pages we read how the estate tax lien is released when a house is sold, so ask the unit directly and ask the title company to request that figure early.

Does the nonresident withholding rule apply to a sale by the estate?

Not for a court-supervised sale. The department's nonresident real property publication lists sales by an estate's personal representative or executor, a conservator or a bankruptcy trustee among the exemptions from escrow withholding.

Other exemptions are narrower:

  • The price, including assumed debt, is $100,000 or less.
  • The tax to be withheld would be under $100 per transferor.
  • The transfer happens through foreclosure or a sheriff's sale.

Outside those cases the escrow agent may ask the seller for Form OR-18-WC. A nonresident heir who has Oregon-source income from the sale also files Form OR-40-N. Keep the form with the estate records rather than sending it to the department.

What should an executor gather before listing an Oregon house?

Collect the date of death, a value for every asset and the paperwork that shows who is acting for the estate. The Department of Revenue says a return is needed at $1 million, so a total of assets drives everything else.

  • A date-of-death valuation of the house, which also supports the heirs' basis.
  • Statements for retirement accounts, bank accounts and any out-of-state property.
  • Proof of who the personal representative is, since that person files Form OR-706.
  • Any prior spouse's estate return that used a marital or QTIP election.

The Estate/Fiduciary Tax Unit is at PO Box 14110, Salem, OR 97309-0910. Its phone lines run 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, except 9 to 11 a.m. on Thursdays and holidays.

Is the Oregon exemption likely to change?

No change has been enacted as of the latest report we found. An August 20, 2026 article from Allen Trust Company says the exemption is held at $1 million, that bills to raise it did not advance, and that a citizen initiative fell short of the signatures needed for the November 3, 2026 ballot.

The same article says observers expect estate tax proposals to get significant attention in the 2027 legislative session. Treat that as a forecast, not a rule. If a family member's death date is near a possible change, a lawyer can say which year's law applies.

For help with an inherited house in Oregon, contact the department's estate team at estate.help.dor@dor.oregon.gov, or the general line at 800-356-4222. This is general information, not legal or tax advice.

More questions about Oregon Estate and Inheritance Tax

What is the Oregon estate tax exemption?

The filing threshold is a gross estate of $1 million or more. Rates start at 10 percent on the taxable estate over $1 million and reach 16 percent above $9.5 million.

Is there an Oregon inheritance tax that heirs pay?

The tax is imposed on the estate, and the executor files Form OR-706. The earlier Form IT-1 was used for deaths before January 1, 2012.

How long does an estate have to file the Oregon return?

For deaths on or after January 1, 2022, the return and payment are due 12 months after death. A six-month extension to file is available, but it does not extend the time to pay.

Does a nonresident who inherits Oregon real estate owe Oregon estate tax?

The estate can owe tax when a nonresident decedent owned Oregon real or tangible personal property and the gross estate reaches $1 million. Only the Oregon property is counted in the ratio.

Can I sell an inherited Oregon house before the estate tax is paid?

Possibly, but we could not confirm the lien release steps from the department's pages, so the title company will want payoff or clearance confirmed first. Contact the Estate/Fiduciary Tax Unit for what applies to your estate.

How does an eviction case work in Oregon?

An Oregon eviction is a court case that decides one thing: who gets possession of the home. The Oregon Judicial Department describes it as an action by a landlord to remove a tenant from a rented dwelling, and it covers houses, apartments, mobile homes and floating homes alike. Back rent and damage claims are not decided in that case.

A landlord has to use the court. The Coos and Curry court self-help page says private eviction help is not permitted and that removing a tenant without a court order is illegal. For a house owner who is thinking about a sale, that rule matters because it sets the pace for everything that follows.

  • The landlord serves a written notice and waits for the notice period to end.
  • The landlord files a complaint and summons with a copy of the notice.
  • A first appearance is set, and the tenant answers or settles.
  • If the case is contested, the court holds a trial.
  • After a judgment for possession, the landlord asks for a notice of restitution and, if needed, a writ of execution carried out by the sheriff.

What are the usual deadlines from filing to move-out?

Most Oregon eviction cases reach a first appearance within about one to two weeks of filing, and a contested trial follows within about another two to four weeks. The numbers below come from the state statute and from court pages in two different counties, so local practice can differ slightly.

StepTimingWhere it comes from
First appearance, most casesAbout one week after filingOregon Law Help
First appearance, nonpaymentAbout two weeks after filingOregon Law Help
First appearance, Multnomah CountyTypically 7 to 14 days out, or 15 to 21 days for certain nonpayment casesMultnomah court page
First appearance, Coos County7 to 15 days after filingCoos court page
Written answerSame day as the first appearanceORS 105.137
Trial, nonpayment claims15 to 30 days after the appearanceORS 105.137
Trial, other claimsNo later than 15 days after the appearanceORS 105.137
Judgment valid for restitution60 daysMultnomah court page
Writ must be servedWithin 30 days of issuanceMultnomah court page

The text of ORS 105.137 adds a protection for the tenant. If trial slips past those windows and the delay is not the landlord's doing, the court can order the tenant to pay accruing rent into court after a hearing finds that order fair.

What happens at the first appearance?

At the first appearance the case ends in a default judgment, a dismissal, a settlement, or a trial date. If the landlord shows up and the tenant does not, the court can enter a judgment of restitution for the landlord. If the tenant shows up and the landlord does not, the tenant can get a dismissal and costs.

An unrepresented tenant who wants to fight the case must file a written answer on the court form and serve the landlord the same day, according to ORS 105.137. In Coos County the answer is due by 4:00 p.m. that day, along with a fee or a request to defer it. The form lists defenses such as missing repairs, retaliation, a defective notice, and status as a victim of domestic violence or stalking.

A settlement is also possible at this stage. The Multnomah page explains that parties can reach an agreement at any point and ask a judge to approve it. If the tenant then breaks the agreement, the landlord can file a declaration of non-compliance and ask for a judgment of restitution.

How must an Oregon eviction notice be delivered?

A written notice under the landlord-tenant chapter can be delivered by hand, sent by first class mail, or, only if the written rental agreement allows it, mailed and attached to the door. Email counts only when the parties signed a separate written addendum after the tenant moved in.

Mailing adds time. Under ORS 90.155, a notice sent by first class mail has its compliance or termination period extended by three days, and the notice has to say so. The notice also has to give the right number of days, because a defective notice is one of the defenses listed on the tenant's answer form. A termination notice sent by email must also go by first class mail.

For a house owner, the practical point is simple. The date the notice was delivered, and how, should be written down before anything is filed. Those records also tell a buyer exactly where the case stands.

When can a landlord use a 24-hour notice?

A 24-hour written notice is allowed only for serious acts listed in ORS 90.396, and the notice must name the act and the date and time the tenancy ends. The statute covers a tenant, someone under the tenant's control, or in some cases the tenant's pet.

  • Seriously threatening or inflicting substantial injury on someone who is not a tenant.
  • Recklessly creating a serious risk of substantial injury to a non-tenant on the premises.
  • Inflicting substantial injury on a neighbor nearby.
  • Intentionally causing substantial damage to the premises.
  • Giving substantially false information about a criminal conviction on the rental application, if the landlord ends the tenancy within 30 days of finding out.
  • Committing an act described as outrageous in the extreme, such as unlawful drug manufacture or distribution, burglary or a bias crime.

The statute text also says a Court of Appeals decision requires the actual date and time to appear in the notice. Pet-related notices must describe the tenant's right to cure by removing the pet.

What is a landlord not allowed to do during an eviction?

A landlord may not change the locks, remove the tenant, or shut off essential services, and may not seriously threaten to do any of those things. ORS 90.375 lists lockouts and the willful loss of heat, water, hot water or electricity.

The remedy is costly for the owner. The tenant can seek an order to return to the home, and can end the rental agreement and recover up to two months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater. The tenant does not have to get an injunction or move back in first. Owners who are tempted to speed up a vacancy before a sale should read that section carefully.

What happens to belongings left in the house?

After a tenancy ends, the landlord must give written notice before storing or selling anything the tenant left, and then wait out a response period. ORS 90.425 sets five days after hand delivery or eight days after mailing for ordinary personal property, and 45 days for a manufactured dwelling or floating home.

The statute also lets a landlord dispose of low-value items without a sale. The thresholds are $1,000 for ordinary property, $4,000 for a recreational vehicle and $8,000 for a manufactured dwelling or floating home. The rule applies when a tenant has been gone seven days after a court eviction order that was not carried out, and when the landlord has regained possession from the sheriff after a writ.

A landlord who follows the steps in good faith has a full defense to claims for the lost items. One who does not can owe up to twice the tenant's actual damages. Any sale that depends on an empty house has to wait for that notice period to run.

How do eviction rules affect selling a rented house?

The court pages cited here do not say a pending eviction blocks a sale, but the open case and the tenant's rights stay tied to the house. Possession and notice defects matter to any buyer, and the court will not rule on back rent in the same case.

  • Eviction court decides possession only. A claim for unpaid rent or damage goes to small claims if it is $10,000 or less, according to the Multnomah court page.
  • A judgment of restitution is good for 60 days, so a sale timeline built around move-out should account for it.
  • The sheriff, not the landlord, carries out the writ.
  • A defective notice is a listed defense, so the notice should be checked before a case is filed.

Owners with a tenant in place, a case in progress, or a house full of old belongings sometimes choose a buyer who will take the property as it stands, with the tenant situation unresolved. That avoids spending months on court steps before a sale. Contact us if you want to talk through the house and the lease.

More questions about Oregon Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does an eviction take in Oregon?

A contested case often runs several weeks from filing to trial. The first appearance usually comes about one to two weeks after filing, and ORS 105.137 puts a trial for nonpayment 15 to 30 days after that appearance. Notice periods before filing, plus the time for a notice of restitution and a writ, add more time.

Can I evict a tenant myself in Oregon without going to court?

No. Changing locks, removing a tenant or cutting off utilities is prohibited by ORS 90.375, and a tenant can recover up to two months of rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. A landlord has to win a judgment and use the court process.

What if the tenant does not show up to the first appearance?

The court may enter a default judgment of restitution for the landlord. Oregon Law Help warns tenants that missing the date can lead to an automatic loss and an eviction on their record, though a tenant with a good reason can ask to set the judgment aside.

How long does a landlord have to store a tenant's belongings?

The tenant gets a written notice and then a response period of at least five days after hand delivery or eight days after mailing for ordinary property. Items worth $1,000 or less, or so little that storage and sale would cost more than a sale brings, may be disposed of under ORS 90.425.

Can I sell a house while an eviction is pending in Oregon?

The court pages we reviewed do not say a pending case blocks a sale, but the case and the tenant's rights stay with the property. A buyer will want the notice, proof of service and court file, and a timeline should account for the 60 days a judgment stays good for restitution. Check with a lawyer or title company on your facts.

What the official sources say

  • A quitclaim deed conveys whatever title or interest the grantor has at the date of the deed, and does not transfer after-acquired title or operate as estoppel. (ORS 93.865(2); source)
  • A grantee under a quitclaim deed is not denied good faith purchaser status solely because of the deed form. (ORS 93.865(3); source)
  • The statutory form states the true consideration and includes the ORS 93.040(1) statement. (ORS 93.865(1); source)
  • The tax statement address line is required on conveyance instruments. (ORS 93.260; source)
  • County clerks charge additional recording fees of $1, $10 and $60 per instrument (on top of the ORS 205.320 base fee). (ORS 205.323(1); source)
  • Deeds must state where tax statements are to be sent; omission does not invalidate the conveyance. (ORS 93.260; source)
  • Contracts to convey fee title at a time more than 12 months out must be acknowledged and recorded within 15 days. (ORS 93.635(1); source)

What does a quitclaim deed actually transfer in Oregon?

It transfers whatever interest the grantor has on the date of the deed, and nothing more. ORS 93.865 gives a short statutory form in which the grantor "releases and quitclaims" all right, title and interest in the described property.

The statute adds that legal and equitable interests both pass, that title the grantor acquires later does not pass, and that the deed does not work as an estoppel. A grantee does not lose good faith purchaser status just because the title came by quitclaim.

Oregon has two other statutory deed forms, and the differences show where a quitclaim fits.

DeedStatuteWhat the grantor promises
Warranty deedORS 93.850Grantor is seized of the estate, the property is free of encumbrances except as stated, and the grantor will defend title against lawful claims. After-acquired title passes.
Special warranty deedORS 93.855Same effect, but the encumbrance promise covers only what the grantor created or allowed, and the warranty covers claims by, through or under the grantor.
Quitclaim deedORS 93.865No covenants. Conveys the grantor's interest on the deed date, whatever it is.

When is a quitclaim deed a reasonable tool?

It works best between people who already know the title history, such as spouses, parents and children, or co-owners sorting out who holds what. Because the grantor makes no covenants, the grantee is relying on the grantor's actual interest and nothing else.

Common uses include:

  • Adding or removing a spouse or family member from a deed
  • Moving a house into or out of a family trust
  • Clearing a possible claim from someone who may have had an interest
  • Splitting up co-owned property after a separation

A federal statute helps some of these transfers. Under 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(d), a lender may not enforce a due-on-sale clause on a home of fewer than five units for transfers such as one to a spouse or children, one to a relative after the borrower dies, one under a divorce decree, or one into a living trust where the borrower stays a beneficiary and keeps occupancy. That law speaks to the lender's clause only, so the other terms of the loan are worth reading separately.

What must an Oregon deed include before the county will record it?

Four items come up most often, and one of them can block recording. The consideration statement in ORS 93.030 has to appear on the face of an instrument that conveys fee title, and a county recording officer may not accept the instrument for recording without it.

  • Consideration. The true and actual consideration paid, written on the deed (ORS 93.030).
  • Mandatory notice. The all-caps statement in ORS 93.040(1) telling the person transferring title to inquire about their rights, and stating that the instrument does not allow use of the property in violation of land use laws. An omission leads to an action only if the buyer would not have accepted the deed without it.
  • Tax statement address. The line beginning "Until a change is requested, all tax statements shall be sent to the following address" (ORS 93.260). Leaving it out does not invalidate the conveyance.
  • Legal description. ORS 93.600 allows a subdivision, lot and block, plat parcel, metes and bounds, or a book and page reference. A tax lot number alone is not adequate.

Deeds also have to be signed by the grantors and acknowledged before a judge, justice of the peace or notary within the state (ORS 93.410). No seal is required. Any restriction that bars use or sale based on race, religion or similar characteristics is void under ORS 93.270.

What are the recording rules and fees at the Oregon county clerk?

The clerk records deeds and mortgages affecting real property under ORS 205.130, and the fees are set in statute. The base fee under ORS 205.320 is $5 for each page, with a $5 minimum, and a page is one side of a sheet no larger than 14 by 8.5 inches.

Three more charges come on top of that under ORS 205.323: $1 for the Oregon Land Information System, $10 split among the county, the clerk and the assessment and taxation fund, and $60 to the assessment and taxation fund. Some filings, such as satisfactions of judgment, are exempt.

ItemRule
Type size10-point or larger (ORS 205.232)
Paper sizeNo larger than 14 inches by 8 1/2 inches
First pageTransaction names, party names, delivery contact, plus consideration and tax statement information for fee conveyances (ORS 205.234)
Missing first-page itemsA cover sheet can be attached and recorded with the instrument
Date of recordThe date of recordation, with the day, hour and minute noted by the clerk (ORS 205.180)

After recording, the clerk returns the instrument to the person who recorded it or is authorized to receive it.

Why does recording order matter when a deed is signed but not recorded?

An unrecorded deed can lose to a later buyer. ORS 93.640 says an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good faith purchaser for value whose instrument is recorded first.

That is why prompt recording matters. If a family keeps a signed quitclaim in a drawer, a second deed from the same grantor can end up ahead of it in line. ORS 93.620 treats an instrument as recorded at the time the clerk certifies, and the county clerk keeps indexes listing the names of all parties (ORS 93.630).

A memorandum can be recorded in place of the full instrument. It must state the date, the parties, a legal description and the nature of the interest, and be signed and acknowledged. A memorandum of a fee conveyance must also state the consideration.

Does Oregon charge a transfer tax on a deed?

Oregon bars new real estate transfer taxes. Voters approved Measure 79 on November 6, 2012, by 58.89 percent to 41.11 percent. Ballotpedia describes the amendment as prohibiting the state and local governments from taxing, charging or assessing the transfer of an interest in real property, or measuring a charge by the price paid.

It exempted any tax, fee or assessment already in effect and operative on December 31, 2009. A seller or grantor should still budget for recording charges, any title or escrow charges, and the county fees above. Those charges apply to a family quitclaim the same way they apply to any other deed.

How are co-owners treated when a deed names more than one person?

A deed to two or more people creates a tenancy in common unless it clearly says the owners have a right of survivorship. A deed to spouses married to each other creates a tenancy by the entirety unless it says otherwise. Under ORS 93.180 and 93.190, joint tenancy is abolished except for conveyances to trustees or personal representatives.

That matters for quitclaims between family members. A quitclaim to a spouse and a child without careful wording leaves a tenancy in common, and each owner's share can pass to that owner's own heirs. When the house is later sold, each co-owner's interest has to be conveyed.

Title also passes at death in a way a quitclaim cannot change. Under ORS 114.215, a decedent's title vests in the heirs or devisees, subject to administration and sale by the personal representative. A deed signed by one heir before probate conveys only that heir's interest.

What mistakes make a quitclaim deed useless for a sale?

Most failures come from skipping a statutory step or expecting the deed to do more than the statute says.

  • Leaving out the consideration statement, which keeps the clerk from recording it
  • Describing the house by tax lot number alone
  • Using paper or type that does not meet the recording size rules
  • Forgetting to record, so a later recorded deed wins
  • Assuming a quitclaim fixes defects or liens that existed before it, when it passes only the grantor's interest
  • Signing for an estate asset without court authority

A quitclaim can be useful in a cash sale when the seller needs to clean up a name on the title before closing. It is not a way to hand over title the grantor does not hold.

More questions about Oregon Quitclaim Deed

Does an Oregon quitclaim deed need to be notarized?

Yes. ORS 93.410 requires deeds to be signed by the grantors and acknowledged before a judge, justice of the peace or notary public in the state. A seal is not required.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Oregon?

The base fee is $5 per page with a $5 minimum, plus $1, $10 and $60 added by ORS 205.323. A county clerk's office can confirm the current total for your page count.

Is there an Oregon transfer tax on a quitclaim deed?

Oregon does not allow new transfer taxes after Measure 79 passed in 2012, except for any that were already operating on December 31, 2009. Recording and other filing fees still apply.

Can a quitclaim deed remove someone from a mortgage?

A quitclaim deed changes who holds title, because ORS 93.865 passes the grantor's interest. The sources reviewed for this page do not say it changes who owes the loan, so ask the lender. Federal law on due-on-sale clauses, 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3(d), covers lender enforcement for certain family transfers.

What is the difference between a quitclaim and a warranty deed in Oregon?

A warranty deed under ORS 93.850 carries promises about ownership, encumbrances and defending title, and passes later-acquired title. A quitclaim under ORS 93.865 carries none of those promises and passes only the grantor's interest on the date of the deed.

Oregon Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Oregon rules with an attorney.

Which Oregon law creates the transfer on death deed?

Oregon's transfer on death deed comes from the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, found at ORS 93.948 to 93.979. The legislature passed it as chapter 212 of the 2011 Oregon Laws, effective January 1, 2012.

The act applies to a deed made before or after that date as long as the owner dies on or after January 1, 2012. It also says it does not affect other methods of transferring property that Oregon law already allows, so a will, a trust or a joint ownership arrangement can still be used.

Under the definitions in ORS 93.949, the transferor is a living individual who signs the deed, and the property is a real estate interest located in Oregon. The beneficiary is whoever receives the property through the deed. A deed can name primary beneficiaries and alternates, who take only if no primary beneficiary survives or qualifies (ORS 93.953).

Oregon transfer on death deed rules at a glance

QuestionAnswer in the statuteSection
When does the beneficiary get the property?At the owner's death, not beforeORS 93.953, 93.967
Must it be recorded?Yes, before the owner dies, in the deed records of the county where the property sitsORS 93.961
Does the beneficiary need to accept it or give anything?No notice, delivery, acceptance or consideration is requiredORS 93.963
Can the owner change their mind?Yes, even if the deed says otherwiseORS 93.955
Time to contest capacity, fraud or undue influence18 months after the owner's deathORS 93.959
Time for estate to reach the property for creditor claims18 months after the owner's deathORS 93.973
Effect of divorce after recordingGifts to the former spouse are revoked unless the deed shows a different intentORS 93.981

What must an Oregon transfer on death deed contain?

It must carry the essential elements and formalities of a recordable lifetime deed, say that the transfer happens at the owner's death, and name the beneficiary. ORS 93.961 voids a designation that names beneficiaries only as members of a class.

The statute also gives an optional fill-in form at ORS 93.975. A deed on that form includes these items:

  • The names and mailing addresses of the owners signing.
  • A legal description of the property.
  • A primary beneficiary and an alternate beneficiary.
  • The address where the county clerk should send tax statements.
  • A return address for the recorded deed.
  • A statement that the owner can revoke it, and a warning that it must be recorded before death to be effective.
  • Signatures and a notary acknowledgment block.

The form itself urges owners to read carefully and consider talking to a lawyer. A wrong legal description or a missing signature is the kind of mistake nobody notices until it is too late to fix.

How much does it cost to record a transfer on death deed in Oregon?

The fee depends on the county. In Multnomah County, recording a deed costs $86 for the first page and $5 for each additional page.

Multnomah County also lists extra charges that can apply to any deed. A cover page costs $5 if the document lacks blank space for the county's 4 inch by 2 inch recording label. A $20 non-standard fee applies if that cover page does not meet the statutory first-page requirements. Each additional transaction in one document is $5, and so is each additional reference to an assignment, release or satisfaction.

Other Oregon counties set their own schedules. Call the county clerk or recorder where the house sits before you mail a deed, because a rejected document that sits in a drawer helps nobody.

What can the owner still do after signing a transfer on death deed?

The owner keeps full control while alive. ORS 93.967 says the deed does not affect the owner's rights, including the right to transfer or encumber the property, and gives the beneficiary no present interest, even if the beneficiary knows about it.

So the owner can sell the house, refinance it or take out a loan against it. The deed also does not change the rights of the owner's creditors, and it does not change whether the owner or the beneficiary qualifies for public or medical assistance as defined in ORS 414.025. The beneficiary's creditors cannot reach the property either, because the beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest during the owner's life.

To undo the deed, ORS 93.965 allows three recorded options:

  • A new transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one, expressly or through inconsistent terms.
  • A recorded instrument that expressly revokes it, in whole or in part.
  • A lifetime deed that transfers the same interest, to the extent of that transfer.

Any of these must be acknowledged and recorded in the county deed records before the owner dies. A named agent can revoke only if the deed expressly gives that authority. Tearing up or writing on a recorded deed does not work, because the statute says a recorded deed cannot be revoked by an act on the deed itself.

What happens to the house when the owner dies?

The designated beneficiary takes the property subject to everything attached to it, including liens, mortgages and other encumbrances. ORS 93.969 states that the beneficiary takes subject to all conveyances and encumbrances, and that includes state claims for public or medical assistance reimbursement when the probate estate cannot cover them.

Other points from the same section:

  • A beneficiary who does not survive the owner loses the gift. The share does not pass under the deed.
  • With several beneficiaries, each takes an equal, undivided share with no right of survivorship, and a lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to their shares.
  • If the owner held title as a joint tenant, a surviving joint owner takes first, and the deed takes effect only when the last surviving joint owner dies.
  • The transfer carries no covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says it does.

A beneficiary can also give up the inheritance. ORS 93.971 lets a beneficiary disclaim all or part of the interest, and it sends the procedure to ORS 105.623 through 105.649.

Can the deed be challenged, and can creditors reach the property?

Yes to both, but only within 18 months after the owner's death. Capacity to make or revoke a transfer on death deed is the same as capacity to make a will, and a deed or revocation obtained by fraud, duress or undue influence is void (ORS 93.959). Anyone who wants to raise either issue must start a proceeding within those 18 months.

On debts, ORS 93.973 lets the estate reach transferred property only to the extent the probate estate is not enough. It covers claims allowed or established against the estate under ORS 114.505 to 114.560 or ORS chapter 115, and statutory allowances owed to a surviving spouse or child under ORS 114.015. If the owner signed several deeds, liability is split among those properties in proportion to each one's net value at death.

Divorce matters too. If the owner divorces or has the marriage annulled after recording, ORS 93.981 revokes the provisions for the former spouse, treating that person as if they had died first. The deed can say otherwise.

What does a transfer on death deed mean for selling an Oregon house?

If the owner is alive, the owner can sell the house like any other. The deed gives the beneficiary no say, and a sale ends the owner's interest, so there is nothing left for the deed to transfer.

If the owner has died, the beneficiary receives the property without a probate transfer, but the 18 month windows in ORS 93.959 and ORS 93.973 are the dates to raise with a title company or attorney before closing a sale. A beneficiary who inherits a house with a mortgage, repair needs or tax bills takes it as-is with those attached.

Many beneficiaries live out of town and do not want to manage an inherited house. We buy Oregon houses as-is for cash, and you can ask us for an offer once you have the recorded deed and the death certificate in hand. A local attorney or the title company should confirm the steps for your county.

More questions about Oregon Transfer on Death Deed

Does a transfer on death deed avoid probate in Oregon?

It can pass the house outside probate, because the transfer happens at death under the deed. The estate can still reach the property for creditor claims if the probate estate is not enough, for up to 18 months after death under ORS 93.973.

Does the beneficiary have to sign or accept an Oregon TOD deed?

No. ORS 93.963 says the deed does not need notice to, delivery to, or acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, and it needs no consideration.

Can I sell my house after recording a transfer on death deed?

Yes. Under ORS 93.967 the deed does not limit your right to sell or borrow against the property while you are alive, and the beneficiary has no present interest.

How do I cancel an Oregon transfer on death deed?

Record a new deed, a revocation instrument, or a lifetime deed of the same interest, each acknowledged and recorded in the county deed records before you die (ORS 93.965). Marking up the recorded deed does not revoke it.

Where do I record a transfer on death deed in Oregon?

In the deed records of the county clerk's office for the county where the property is located (ORS 93.961). In Multnomah County the fee is $86 for the first page and $5 for each added page.

Does Oregon tax the profit when you sell a house?

Yes. Oregon taxes profit from a home sale as part of income, because state law is meant to measure taxable income the same way the federal Internal Revenue Code does (ORS 316.007). The result is that gain on a house you sell flows onto your Oregon return, and the federal home sale exclusion helps on both.

Oregon's statute lists one rate table for taxable income, and the sources we opened do not set a separate state rate for long-term gains. Residents are taxed under the table below, and the lower brackets are adjusted each year for inflation.

Taxable income (base schedule)Oregon tax
Up to $2,0004.75 percent
$2,000 to $5,000$95 plus 6.75 percent of the excess over $2,000
$5,000 to $125,000$298 plus 8.75 percent of the excess over $5,000
Over $125,000$10,798 plus 9.9 percent of the excess over $125,000

The top bracket is not indexed. A large gain on a house can push part of a year's income into the 9.9 percent bracket, so the order and size of other income in the sale year matters.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work for an Oregon seller?

You can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on your main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. To qualify you or your spouse must have owned the home for at least 24 months within the five years before the sale, and each spouse claiming the larger amount must have used it as a main home for at least 24 months in that window.

The IRS also says you generally cannot claim the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home sold in the previous two years. If you receive a Form 1099-S you must report the sale even when all the gain is excludable, and any taxable part goes on Schedule D and Form 8949.

  • Owned and lived in the house at least 24 months of the last 60: the exclusion is likely available.
  • Rented it out for most of the last five years: the use test may fail.
  • Sold another home with an exclusion within two years: the limit may apply.

Our team does not give tax advice, so a preparer should run the actual dates, especially if you moved out before selling.

What happens to gain above the exclusion?

It is taxed at the federal level as a capital gain and at the Oregon level as income. Property held more than one year produces a long-term gain, and the IRS lists 0, 15 and 20 percent long-term rates, with the 2025 thresholds starting at $48,350 for a single filer on the 0 percent rate and $96,700 for joint filers.

Those thresholds are labeled by the IRS as 2025 figures, so check the current year before you plan. Two other items matter for real estate:

  • Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from selling real property is capped at a 25 percent rate. A preparer can tell you whether past rental depreciation creates any.
  • Higher earners may also owe the net investment income tax, which the IRS covers under Topic 559.

Short-term gains, from a house held one year or less, are taxed as ordinary income. An Oregon resident then adds the state tax on top of the federal result.

How do you work out your gain on an Oregon house?

Gain is the amount you realize on the sale minus your adjusted basis. Basis starts as the price you paid plus purchase costs, goes up with improvements that add value, and goes down with depreciation and with insurance reimbursements for casualty losses.

Basis works differently if you did not buy the house. For inherited property, IRS Publication 551 says basis is generally the fair market value at the date of death, or the alternate valuation date if the personal representative made that election. A house inherited and sold soon after often shows little gain for that reason.

ItemEffect on basis
Purchase price and closing costsSets the starting figure
Improvements that add valueIncrease basis
Depreciation on a rentalDecreases basis
Casualty insurance reimbursementsDecrease basis
InheritanceFair market value at date of death, generally

Keep closing statements and receipts for large projects, such as a new roof or a kitchen, because the sale price is only half of the equation.

What if you live outside Oregon and sell Oregon real estate?

Oregon taxes nonresidents on income from Oregon sources, and gain from selling Oregon real property counts (ORS 316.127). Full-year nonresidents use the same rate table on that Oregon-source income, and a nonresident return is Form OR-40-N.

The escrow agent may have to withhold Oregon tax at closing. The Department of Revenue says the amount is the least of four percent of the consideration, the net proceeds, or eight percent of the gain includible in Oregon taxable income. The transferor completes the seller sections of Form OR-18-WC, signs it and gives it to the escrow agent, who completes the rest. You keep the form with your tax records and do not send it to the department.

A sale is exempt from withholding when:

  • The consideration, including assumed debt, is $100,000 or less.
  • The home is your personal residence and no federal income tax is owed on the sale.
  • A credit for tax paid to the home state means no Oregon tax is likely.
  • The tax to be withheld is under $100 per transferor.
  • The transfer avoids foreclosure with no additional payment, or occurs through foreclosure or a sheriff's sale.
  • A court-supervised sale occurs, such as one by a personal representative or bankruptcy trustee.

Withholding is not the final tax. A nonresident still files Form OR-40-N when Oregon gross income exceeds the filing threshold, even when the sale was exempt, and the withheld amount is credited on that return. Oregon residents are exempt transferors.

When does Oregon expect payment on the tax from a home sale?

For a resident, the tax is settled on the annual Oregon return, and the Department of Revenue says estimated payments are generally needed if you expect to owe $1,000 or more after credits and withholding. A large gain in a single year can meet that test, so some sellers make an estimated payment in the year of the sale.

A short plan helps:

  1. Gather the purchase documents, improvement receipts and the closing statement.
  2. Estimate gain and subtract any exclusion you qualify for.
  3. Compare expected tax with withholding and credits for the year.
  4. Decide whether an estimated payment is needed before the next quarter's date.

The Department of Revenue can be reached at 503-378-4988 or 800-356-4222 or by email at questions.dor@dor.oregon.gov. Estimated tax rules for nonresidents are narrower, since they figure it only on income that is subject to Oregon withholding, from an Oregon business or lottery winnings over $600, so a nonresident should read the instructions on the department's website carefully.

How does a cash sale change the tax picture?

A cash sale does not change the tax rules. The gain is figured from the same sale price, basis and exclusion, and a title or escrow company still runs the closing, so the withholding steps above still happen there.

Sellers who are weighing a quick as-is sale often ask the same questions:

  • Will I owe Oregon tax? It depends on your gain, exclusion and residency.
  • Do I need to report the sale if the gain is fully excluded? You do if you received Form 1099-S.
  • Does an out-of-state address trigger withholding? It can, unless an exemption applies.

This page is general information and not tax advice, so confirm the numbers with a tax professional or the Department of Revenue.

More questions about Oregon Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Oregon have a capital gains tax on home sales?

Oregon taxes gain on a home sale as part of income, with rates from 4.75 percent to 9.9 percent under ORS 316.037. The federal exclusion of $250,000 or $500,000 can remove all or part of the gain first.

What is the Oregon withholding on a nonresident home sale?

The escrow agent withholds the least of four percent of the consideration, the net proceeds, or eight percent of the gain includible in Oregon income, unless an exemption applies. Form OR-18-WC documents the calculation.

Do I report a home sale if the gain is under the exclusion?

Yes, if you received Form 1099-S, the sale must be reported even when all gain is excludable. Report any taxable part on Schedule D and Form 8949.

Is gain on an inherited house taxed in Oregon?

Only gain over the stepped-up basis is taxed, since basis is generally the fair market value at the date of death. A sale soon after inheriting often shows little gain.

Who do I call with questions about Oregon tax on a sale?

Call the Oregon Department of Revenue at 503-378-4988 or 800-356-4222, or email questions.dor@dor.oregon.gov.

What the official sources say

  • A judgment debtor may redeem property sold at an execution sale within 180 days after the sale date. (ORS 18.964(1); source)
  • A lien claimant may redeem within 60 days after the sale date. (ORS 18.964(2); source)
  • A judgment creditor may bid orally or submit a written bid at least 48 hours before the sale, not exceeding the judgment amount plus recoverable sale costs. (ORS 18.936; source)
  • The sheriff delivers net sale proceeds to the court administrator, and the court enters an order of distribution. (ORS 18.950(1); source)
  • If a homestead exemption applies, the sheriff may not sell unless the bid exceeds sale costs plus the exemption amount. (ORS 18.395(8); source)
  • A homestead occupied by the debtor may not be sold on execution to satisfy a judgment of $3,000 or less at entry. (ORS 18.395(5); source)
  • Notice of sale must go to the grantor, successors in interest of record, and subsequent lienholders of record. (ORS 86.764(2); source)
  • A trustee's sale forecloses and terminates interests of noticed persons, who may not redeem from the purchaser. (ORS 86.797(1); source)
  • No deficiency action may follow a trustee's sale or judicial foreclosure of a residential trust deed. (ORS 86.797(2); source)
  • Judicial foreclosure of a lien is by suit; a complaint on a residential trust deed must attach resolution-conference compliance documents. (ORS 88.010; source)
  • A judgment of foreclosure orders the property sold; judicial-sale redemption follows execution-sale rules (ORS 18.860 to 18.993). (ORS 88.106; source)
Selling in Oregon?
We buy Oregon houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is the difference between a sheriff sale and a trustee's sale in Oregon?

A sheriff sells the house after a court judgment, while a trustee sells it under a trust deed without a court case. Oregon uses both, and the rules for notice, timing and what follows the sale are different.

TrackWho runs the saleKey facts
Trustee's sale (nonjudicial)The trustee named in the trust deedHeld after 9 a.m. and before 4 p.m. in a county where the property sits (ORS 86.782). Notice is served or mailed at least 120 days ahead (ORS 86.764).
Judicial foreclosureSheriff, after a court judgmentFiled as a suit (ORS 88.010). Sale and redemption follow the execution-sale rules (ORS 88.106).
Execution sale on a money judgmentSheriffPublic oral auction between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. (ORS 18.930).

This page focuses on the sheriff side. The sources are chapters 18, 86 and 88 of the Oregon Revised Statutes.

How does an Oregon sheriff give notice of a real property sale?

In four ways at once: a website, a newspaper, the mail and the property itself. ORS 18.924 sets the steps for a sale of real property.

  • The sheriff posts the notice on the legal notices website for at least 28 days.
  • The notice also runs in a county newspaper once a week for four successive weeks.
  • At least 28 days before the sale, the sheriff mails it to the debtor by first-class and certified mail, and to the debtor's attorney and listed persons by first-class mail.
  • If a street address is given, a copy is posted on the property within seven days after the mailing.

The judgment creditor supplies the list of people who must be told. For real property, ORS 18.918 includes the debtor, any attorney named in the judgment, later lienholders and people who recorded interests from the debtor in a set window. In a foreclosure judgment, the list is the parties to the action. A missed name does not void the sale, but the creditor's certification can draw sanctions.

How does the sale itself work, and can it be postponed?

It is a public oral auction held between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. The judgment creditor must give the sheriff any title report at least 10 days before the first set sale date, and a county may collect a fee at the sale (ORS 18.930).

Several rules limit who buys and how much is sold. The sheriff sells only what is necessary to satisfy the judgment, and the sheriff and deputies cannot buy at the sale or take an interest because of it (ORS 18.934).

Postponements are built into the statute. Under ORS 18.932 the sheriff may postpone if the sale cannot proceed at the noticed time, if there are no buyers, or for other sufficient cause. The sheriff must postpone on the creditor's request, up to the return date. Multiple postponements are allowed, and no new notice of sale is needed.

A date printed on a notice is therefore a starting point, because a creditor's request or other cause can move it.

What happens right after the sheriff sells a house?

The sheriff prepares a certificate of sale, and the purchaser records it in the County Clerk Lien Record. ORS 18.942 says the certificate states whether the property is subject to redemption.

A real property sale is presumed to have been properly conducted unless the debtor or another affected person files an objection within 10 days after the sheriff's return is filed (ORS 18.948). If someone objects, the court holds a hearing and confirms the sale unless the objector shows the sale did not substantially conform to the law and probably caused damage. If the objection is sustained, the property is resold and the sheriff may not accept a bid below the first price.

The purchaser can take possession from the sale date until any redemption, and a tenant with an unexpired lease may stay through the redemption period by paying the greater of the value of use and occupancy or the lease payments (ORS 18.946). For a trustee's sale, the buyer is entitled to possession on the tenth day after the sale (ORS 86.782).

Who can redeem a property after an Oregon sheriff sale, and what does it cost?

The judgment debtor, a mortgagor whose interest was sold, a junior lienholder, or a successor to any of them. ORS 18.963 lists these redeemers, and a person who has conveyed all of their interest to a successor cannot redeem.

The redemption windows are 180 days for the debtor and 60 days for a lien claimant (ORS 18.964). To redeem from the purchaser, the claimant pays the purchase price with interest at nine percent per year from the sale date. Taxes, costs to prevent waste, senior liens and homeowners' association assessments that the purchaser paid are added, each with nine percent interest from the date of payment (ORS 18.966).

Unless the debtor redeems, the sheriff delivers a deed to the certificate holder on request and payment of the statutory fee, as soon as possible (ORS 18.985). A court may order a deed early if the certificate holder has acquired all redemption rights.

What can a homeowner do before a foreclosure sale in Oregon?

A lender on a residential trust deed generally has to offer a resolution conference before it can foreclose. ORS 86.726 says a lender that intends to foreclose a residential trust deed must first request a conference with the borrower, unless it qualifies for a limited exemption based on how few actions it filed the previous year.

The Oregon Housing and Community Services page on the Foreclosure Avoidance Program explains how it works in practice:

  • The Department of Justice oversees the program, and a Mediation Case Manager handles day-to-day operations.
  • Homeowners pay a fee to the case manager, meet a housing counselor, submit documents, and attend the conference with a neutral facilitator.
  • Low-income homeowners may have all but $50 of the fee waived.
  • Housing counselors are free, and OHCS keeps a list of approved agencies.
  • The lender must send a representative with full authority to negotiate, but it does not have to modify the loan.

The statute caps the grantor's fee at $200 and the lender's at $600, with the conference scheduled within 10 days of a request and held within 75 days after notice (ORS 86.729). Missing the fee deadline leads the case manager to cancel the conference and issue a certificate of compliance, after which the lender may go ahead.

Help lines listed on the state page include the Mediation Case Manager at 855-658-6733 and the Department of Justice Consumer Protection Hotline at 877-877-9392 for scam reports.

How do junior lienholders and judicial foreclosure timing affect a sheriff sale?

Junior lienholders have to be named in the suit, or they keep some rights. Under ORS 88.030, a junior holder left out of the case who does not redeem within five years of the sheriff's sale is barred from later action on that interest.

Some other points in chapter 88 matter for owners:

  • Paying the amount due and costs before judgment dismisses the suit. Paying after judgment but before sale ends the judgment's effect for the amount paid (ORS 88.100).
  • A foreclosure judgment is enforced by execution. If the sale falls short, a money award can be enforced like an ordinary judgment (ORS 88.060).
  • For certain purchase-money mortgages, including seller-financed ones and some residential mortgages of $50,000 or less, the judgment remedies for unpaid amounts end at the sale (ORS 88.103).
  • A mortgage lien ends 10 years after the later of maturity, the end of the debt term or an agreed extension, with exceptions (ORS 88.110 and 88.120).

In a trustee's sale, a subsequent lienholder who did not get required notice gets the rights of an omitted junior lienholder in a judicial foreclosure, and those are the exclusive remedies (ORS 86.767).

What does a trustee's sale add to the timeline?

It adds a long runway, plus an extra publication step. Notice of sale must be served on an occupant at least 120 days before the sale, and it must run once a week for four successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation, with the last publication more than 20 days before the sale (ORS 86.774).

The notice states the date, time and place of sale, and the right to reinstate no later than five days before the last date set (ORS 86.771). The sale may be postponed for periods totaling no more than 180 days from the original date, and notice of a new date must be given at least 15 days ahead unless the postponement is two calendar days or less (ORS 86.782).

The trustee delivers the deed within 10 days after the purchaser pays, and the trustee may rescind within 10 calendar days after the sale only on listed grounds, such as a bona fide error.

More questions about Oregon Sheriff Sales

How long do I have to redeem my house after an Oregon sheriff sale?

A judgment debtor has 180 days after the sale. A lien claimant has 60 days. The redemption price is the purchase price plus nine percent yearly interest and any taxes or senior liens the buyer paid (ORS 18.964 and 18.966).

Can an Oregon sheriff sale be postponed?

Yes. The sheriff can postpone if the sale cannot go forward, if there are no buyers, or for other sufficient cause, and must postpone at the creditor's request up to the return date. A postponement does not require a new notice of sale (ORS 18.932).

Where is an Oregon foreclosure sale held?

A trustee's sale must be held in a county where the property is located, between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. A sheriff sale is a public oral auction, also held between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. (ORS 86.782 and 18.930).

Can the sheriff buy the property at the sale?

No. The sheriff and deputies may not buy property at the sale or get any interest in it because of the sale (ORS 18.934).

Is there free help for Oregon homeowners facing foreclosure?

Yes. The state Foreclosure Avoidance Program connects homeowners with free housing counselors and a resolution conference with their lender. The Mediation Case Manager's number is 855-658-6733.

  • The affidavit must describe estate property, including a legal description of any real property, and list heirs, devisees and creditors. (ORS 114.525(1); source)
